Giant Octopus.description: An octopus grown far past natural size that hides by changing the color and texture of its skin, then seizes prey with eight suckered arms.[1]
Giant Octopus.lore:
The giant octopus is the largest octopus species. It lives across the North Pacific, from Japan to Alaska's Aleutian Islands and south to Baja California, in tide pools and in water as deep as 1,500 meters.[1] It is usually reddish, but it can change both its color and the texture of its skin to hide or when threatened.[1]

It lives alone in a den under a boulder or in a rock crevice, sometimes for weeks, and goes out only to hunt, mate or escape danger.[1] It carries clams, crabs, fish and squid back to the den to eat, and the leftover shells pile up at the entrance.[1] When chased, it jets away and leaves a cloud of ink behind to cover its escape.[1]

The suckers on its arms can both feel and taste.[1] The species is known for its intelligence. It navigates by landmarks, uses objects as tools and learns by watching, and captive octopuses have a reputation for escaping their tanks.[1] A female lays tens of thousands of eggs in her den and guards them without leaving even to eat, and she dies while they develop or soon after they hatch.[1] In the wild, the species lives about four and a half to five years.[1]

Mammoth.description: An extinct elephant with long tusks that curve in a spiral, a domed head and a back that slopes down from high shoulders.[1]
Mammoth.lore:
Mammoths were elephants. The elephant family arose in Africa about seven million years ago and split into three lines, which led to African elephants, Asian elephants and mammoths.[1] The oldest known mammoth fossils are teeth from South Africa, about five million years old.[1] About 3.5 million years ago, mammoths spread out of Africa through the Middle East and across Eurasia, and about 1.5 million years ago they crossed the Bering land bridge into North America.[1]

Their tusks curved in a spiral, where a living elephant's tusks bend in one simple arc.[1] Early mammoths mostly ate leaves from shrubs and trees. Later ones grazed on grass, as cold, dry grasslands spread across Asia.[1] Not every mammoth was shaggy: the woolly mammoth had a thick coat, but how much hair the earlier species had is not known.[1]

The woolly mammoth was the last to survive. It was still widespread 20,000 years ago. Within the next 10,000 years, only small groups were left on islands off Siberia and Alaska, and by 4,000 years ago they were gone.[2]

Swarm of Bats.description: Hundreds of bats that roost together by day in caves, mines and hollow trees, then fill the night air as they hunt by sound.[1][2]
Swarm of Bats.lore:
More than 1,300 species of bats live around the world, more than any other group of mammals except rodents.[1] By day they rest in caves, mines, trees, rock crevices and under bridges, out of reach of predators. Many crowd together in one place, either to raise young in a maternity colony or to sleep through the winter in a hibernaculum.[1]

Bats find their way and their food by echolocation. They call at pitches too high for human ears and listen for the echoes. When a bat closes in on an insect, it speeds its calls into a rapid buzz to pin down where its prey is.[2] Every species has its own pattern of calls.[2]

Some bats eat insects, others prefer fruit or pollen, and a few catch fish. Most have a single pup a year, and some live as long as 35 years.[3]

Tyrannosaurus Rex.description: A two-legged predator about 12 meters long, with a massive skull, small arms and saw-edged teeth strong enough to crush bone.[1]
Tyrannosaurus Rex.lore:
Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the end of the age of dinosaurs, 68 to 66 million years ago, in what is now Canada and the United States. Its name means "tyrant lizard king".[1] A typical adult stood 3.5 to 4 meters tall at the hip and weighed 5 to 7 tonnes, and the largest known individuals passed 8 tonnes.[1]

Its 60 teeth, some up to 20 centimeters long, gave it the strongest bite of any known land animal, three to five times as strong as a lion's.[1] It bit through bone and swallowed it: bone fragments turn up in its fossilized dung, and its tooth marks appear on Triceratops and Edmontosaurus fossils.[1] Much of its brain was given over to smell, which let it track both living prey and carcasses over long distances.[1]

Its small arms are still debated. They may have helped it stand up after a fall, grip food while it was young, or hold a partner during mating.[1] Fossil skin shows scales, and there is no direct evidence that it had feathers.[1] An adult's top speed is estimated at about 22 kilometers an hour.[1]

Wolf.description: A lean wild dog with a coat anywhere from gray to brown, black or white, that hunts in family packs able to kill a moose or a bison.[1]
Wolf.lore:
The wolf is the largest wild member of the dog family. Males can weigh up to about 80 kilograms and reach about two meters from nose to tail tip.[1] Wolves once ranged over more of the Northern Hemisphere than almost any other land mammal, in every kind of habitat except tropical forest.[1]

A pack is a family: a breeding pair and their young, usually five to eight wolves, though packs of more than 30 have been recorded. The pair leads hunts and teaches the young, and a wolf may leave around two years of age to find a mate and start its own pack.[1] A pack holds and defends a territory of anywhere from 130 to 13,000 square kilometers. Wolves can travel up to 200 kilometers in a day and sprint at 55 to 70 kilometers an hour.[2]

A howl carries about ten kilometers. Wolves howl to gather the pack, to start a hunt, to warn off other packs and to guide a lost wolf home.[1] Folklore has long cast the wolf as an animal to fear, and that fear still shapes how people treat wolves today.[1]
